title: Monitor Accountability Act
official_title: To provide for conditions on the appointment of monitors by courts, and for other purposes.
summary: Federal courts must follow new rules when appointing monitors to oversee state and local governments under consent decrees — including fee caps, a 5-year term limit, a one-monitorship-at-a-time restriction, and mandatory public notice before appointment. The Judicial Conference of the United States must issue rules within 180 days, and active monitorships already running 6 or more years must get a new monitor within 180 days and be transferred to a new judge within 1 year.
brief: Sets term limits, fee caps, and public accountability rules for court-appointed monitors overseeing state and local governments under consent decrees.

top_lines.headline: Monitor Term and Appointment Limits
subs: 5-year term limit per court order; no reappointment under the same order after term expires
Monitor may not hold more than one monitorship at a time
Successor monitor may not be employed by the same firm as the prior monitor

top_lines.headline: Fee Caps and Public Accountability
subs: Fees capped at rates set by the Judicial Conference of the United States; pro bono and reduced-rate services explicitly authorized
Annual public accounting of services, fees, and any pro bono work required from each monitor
Court must provide public notice and comment opportunity before appointing any monitor

top_lines.headline: Case Transfer and Retroactivity
subs: Case transferred to a new judge in the same district 6 years after the court order
Existing monitorships of 6+ years: new monitor appointed within 180 days of enactment, case transferred within 1 year

likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 219-204 with only 5 crossover votes — a near party-line result indicating minimal Democratic support. Sponsor Rep. Biggs (R-AZ) had only 2 cosponsors. Consent decree reform is sharply partisan: term limits and fee caps would disrupt ongoing civil rights oversight of police departments, and Democratic senators are expected to oppose unanimously. The Senate 60-vote threshold is not within reach under current conditions.

items.main: Names the Act the “Monitor Accountability Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: The Judicial Conference of the United States must establish rules within 180 days imposing fee caps, a single-monitorship-at-a-time limit, a 5-year term limit with no reappointment under the same court order, and a prohibition on successive monitors sharing employers.
items.detail: Conditions apply to any person appointed by a district court to monitor the conduct of a state or unit of local government. Fee rules must explicitly authorize pro bono and reduced-rate services. Courts must provide public notice and an opportunity for comment before any monitor appointment.

items.main: Cases are transferred to a new judge in the same district 6 years after the court order imposing the monitorship; monitors must submit annual public accountings of services, fees, and pro bono work to the court.
items.detail: For monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years on the date of enactment, a new monitor must be appointed within 180 days and the case transferred within 1 year. The transfer trigger is purely time-based with no assessment of compliance status required.

underreported.summary: The retroactivity clause requires all monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years to appoint a new monitor within 180 days and transfer the case to a new judge within 1 year, regardless of whether the monitored entity is making progress toward compliance.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around appointment conditions for future monitorships, but Section 2(d) immediately disrupts currently active monitorship arrangements without any compliance-status prerequisite.

underreported.summary: Cases transfer to a new judge automatically at exactly 6 years after the court order on a time-based trigger with no assessment of case status, compliance progress, or complexity.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill purpose covers appointment conditions, but the judge-transfer provision operates as a mandatory procedural reset on a fixed schedule independent of whether the monitorship is progressing toward its stated goals.

underreported.summary: A court may only revise a requirement of a monitorship if the subject of the monitorship has not attained "substantial and sustained compliance" with that requirement, and any such revision requires a hearing (Sec. 2(a)(5)(A)-(B)). This is the bill's only compliance-based standard.
underreported.why_unreported: The analysis elsewhere repeatedly frames the bill as having no compliance test — e.g., describing the 6-year transfer and 6-year retroactivity triggers as purely time-based — which is accurate for those specific provisions, but the bill does introduce a compliance standard, narrowly, for court revisions of individual monitorship requirements. Omitting it left readers with the impression that the bill contains no compliance concept anywhere.

criticisms.why: I do rise today in opposition to H.R. 8365, the Monitor Accountability Act. This bill addresses the work of Federal monitors who are appointed by a court to oversee the progress a State or a unit of local government is making after violating Federal law. Often monitors are put in place after there is a finding of serious misconduct, including violations of constitutional rights or actions that jeopardize people's public health, safety, and well-being.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. McBath
featured_quotes.text: I do rise today in opposition to H.R. 8365, the Monitor Accountability Act. This bill addresses the work of Federal monitors who are appointed by a court to oversee the progress a State or a unit of local government is making after violating Federal law. Often monitors are put in place after there is a finding of serious misconduct, including violations of constitutional rights or actions that jeopardize people's public health, safety, and well-being.

gaps: The bill sets a 5-year term limit for monitors but specifies no continuity procedure if no compliant replacement monitor can be identified or appointed before the prior monitor's term expires.

The bill scope covers monitors appointed to oversee state and local governments but does not address monitors appointed in deferred prosecution agreements with private entities or federal contractors, which operate under the same district court rules.

added: Mandatory conditions on federal court appointment of monitors for state and local government oversight (fee caps, 5-year term limit, single-monitorship limit)
Prohibition on successive monitors under the same court order sharing the same employer
Public notice and comment requirement before any monitor appointment
Annual public accounting of monitor fees and services
Mandatory case transfer to a new judge 6 years after the court order
Retroactivity for all monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years: new monitor within 180 days, new judge within 1 year

A court may only revise a monitorship requirement through a hearing, and only where the subject of the monitorship has not attained "substantial and sustained compliance" with that requirement — the bill's sole compliance standard (Sec. 2(a)(5))

modified: Rulemaking authority shifted from the Administrator of the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts to the Judicial Conference of the United States (including the maximum-fee-rate authority)
Rulemaking deadline lengthened from "not later than 90 days" to "not later than 180 days" after the section's effective date
Short title shortened from "Monitor Accountability Act of 2026" to "Monitor Accountability Act"
